Stress urinary incontinence

A sham-controlled GSM trial found lower urinary loss after vaginal PBM, and a controlled trial reported a clinically meaningful questionnaire improvement when PBM was added to pelvic-floor training. Direct SUI trials show mixed results, and a multimodal uncontrolled study cannot isolate the light component.

7directly relevant clinical publications (4 randomized trials, 3 single-arm studies)

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Urinary symptoms in women with GSM: The PBM plus pelvic-floor training group had a 3.06-point greater post-treatment ICIQ-SF improvement than the sham-PBM plus training group; the authors described the change as clinically meaningful, while their abstract characterized the overall between-group urinary-function difference as non-significant (Bezerra et al., 2026, PubMed).

Multimodal home treatment: 84% of 55 women met the study authors’ pad-weight response definition after a device combining light, heat, and vibration. The PBM contribution cannot be isolated (de la Torre et al., 2017, PubMed).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term urinary-loss reduction in women with GSM

Low for SUI-specific continence outcomes across protocols

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A sham-controlled GSM trial found lower urinary loss after vaginal PBM, and a controlled trial reported a clinically meaningful questionnaire improvement when PBM was added to pelvic-floor training. Direct SUI trials show mixed results, and a multimodal uncontrolled study cannot isolate the light component.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven relevant human publications were identified: four randomized trials and three uncontrolled studies. Four directly enrolled women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI) or included a defined SUI subgroup. Three additional reports were mapped from genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), which can include urinary symptoms but is not identical to stress leakage. In one 2025 pilot, the SUI and GSM subgroups overlapped by five participants and must not be counted as separate cohorts. No animal or separate in-vitro study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

A randomized, double-blind trial in 22 women combined pelvic-floor strengthening with an 808-nm near-infrared laser. The PBM group had better immediate pelvic-floor muscle performance after the exercise program. This is a measured short-term muscle outcome, not proof of fewer leakage episodes over time (da Silva et al., 2023, PMID 38017192).

In a three-arm randomized trial, 33 women received Pilates with sham PBM and static magnetic field, Pilates with active PBM and static magnetic field, or active PBM and static magnetic field alone. The authors found no significant between-group differences in the main pelvic-floor and urinary outcomes, despite within-group changes (De Marchi et al., 2023, PMID 36769752).

A newer sham-controlled trial in postmenopausal women with GSM and urinary incontinence reported lower urinary loss and better ICIQ-SF scores after vaginal PBM. A separate controlled GSM trial combining PBM with pelvic-floor training reported improved urinary symptoms, although its conclusions describe the between-group urinary-function difference as non-significant. These findings concern urinary outcomes in GSM populations and do not establish effectiveness across all causes of SUI (Pereira et al., 2026, PMID 42060269; Bezerra et al., 2026, PMID 42566226).

Three uncontrolled studies offer additional context. A 41-participant pilot reported improved questionnaire scores in its SUI subgroup, but five participants also belonged to the GSM subgroup, and there was no control group (Wu et al., 2025, PMID 40486198). A 27-woman GSM study also reported improvement in lower-urinary-tract symptoms after intravaginal PBM without a comparator (Wu et al., 2026, PMID 42329990). In a 55-woman SUI study, most participants met the authors’ pad-weight response definition, but the home device combined light with heat and vibration, so the PBM contribution cannot be separated (de la Torre et al., 2017, PMID 28035444).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for urinary incontinence was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue experiment directly examining SUI outcomes was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols included 808-nm near-infrared laser light, 640-nm red plus 875/905-nm near-infrared LEDs with a static magnetic field, and 660-nm red light delivered by an intravaginal probe. The exercise-associated 808-nm trial used 3 J per point at 100 mW, while the three-arm PBM/sMF trial delivered 54.15 J per session over 24 sessions in 12 weeks. The 2025 pilot used 660-nm red light at 18.17 mW/cm² and 32.4 J/cm² for 30 minutes weekly over eight weeks. A 2026 GSM trial used 808-nm near-infrared light at 4 J per point across eight vulvar sites for four weekly sessions. A later 660-nm pilot used 30-minute pulsed sessions eight times over eight weeks. The home device combined 662-nm red and 855-nm near-infrared light with heat and vibration. Delivery was intravaginal, sometimes alongside exercise. Doses and schedules differ, and no study establishes a preferred protocol.

Interpretation

The strongest direct finding is a short-term urinary-loss improvement in a small GSM-related trial. Direct SUI studies show better immediate muscle performance in one trial, no between-group advantage in another, and uncontrolled improvements with multimodal devices. The evidence supports further testing of specific protocols and populations, while leaving durable continence benefit uncertain.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Four small randomized trials include both stress-incontinence cohorts and women with genitourinary syndrome, while three uncontrolled studies add symptom and pad-test observations. One GSM trial found less urinary leakage than sham, but direct SUI trials do not consistently show an added effect. Independent sham-controlled trials should measure leakage and daily function over longer follow-up.
